title: How to Find the Font on a Website in Chrome
description: Identify a website’s real rendered font, size, weight, and line height in Chrome. Learn why font stacks and screenshot guesses can mislead you.
keyword: how to find font on website
body:
To find the font on a website, right-click the text, choose Inspect, and open Elements → Computed in Chrome DevTools. Check font-family, then scroll to Rendered Fonts to identify the typeface actually used. Record the size, weight, and line height too: the family name alone will not reproduce the typography.

This guide is for live, selectable website text. If the lettering is inside a photograph, screenshot, or outlined logo, you need image-based identification instead. Start by checking which kind of material you have.

Choose a method for the text you have

What you can accessStart hereWhat to verify
Selectable live textChrome’s element inspectorRendered font and computed styles
A screenshot or photoAn image-based font matching serviceCandidate matches, not an exact CSS declaration
A logo built with SVG pathsBrand guidelines or the original design fileWhether the lettering was customized
Your own source projectFont declarations and component stylesWhich files load in the browser

For example, a heading can look like ordinary text while sitting inside a hero image. Try selecting a word. If the browser selects the entire image instead, inspecting that image will not reveal the font used to create its pixels.

Inspect the exact text element

  1. Open the page and wait for its text to settle.
  2. Right-click the heading or paragraph you want, then choose Inspect.
  3. In Elements, select the smallest element containing that text. A nested span may have different styling from its parent.
  4. Open Computed and search for font. Note family, size, style, and weight.
  5. Clear the filter and inspect Rendered Fonts near the bottom of the panel.

Chrome documents the Rendered Fonts section in its font inspection example. That section helps distinguish a local font from a web font. If the interface differs in your Chrome version, look for the Computed panel within Elements.

Why the first font name may be wrong

A declaration such as font-family: "Studio Sans", Arial, sans-serif is a preference list. It does not prove that Studio Sans loaded. The browser may use a fallback, and different characters can come from different fonts. MDN’s font-family reference explains the ordered selection and character-level fallback.

Consider a card with English text followed by an emoji. Treat the emoji font as a separate observation, not evidence that the whole card uses it. Similarly, a page may use one family for headings and another for forms. Sample each role you intend to recreate.

Record a useful typography specimen

Use a short record like this original example when moving from inspection to implementation. These values are illustrative, not measurements of another website:

Role: card title
Sample: A calmer way to work
Rendered family: Inter
Weight: 600
Size: 24px
Line height: 30px
Letter spacing: -0.3px
Container width: 320px
State: desktop, default

The container width matters because it changes where a line wraps. A correct font inside the wrong width may look like a wrong font. Save the exact sample text, viewport, and the state of the component so you can repeat the comparison.

Download the typography audit worksheet and fill one row per role. If you are collecting more than type, use the website design-system audit to keep the measurements together.

Troubleshoot a font that still looks different

  • Wrong weight: compare the actual weight, not just a “bold” label in your editor.
  • Wrong line breaks: match text, width, font size, and letter spacing before changing the family.
  • Late loading: reload and watch whether the text changes after the initial render.
  • Different device: check the same page on the device where the mismatch occurs.
  • Different state: inspect the element after opening its menu or changing its tab.

When the computed value is surprising, trace the matching CSS rule and inherited styles. Our CSS inspection workflow explains how to find the declaration behind a visible result.

Turn the observation into your own type system

Choose a small set of text roles: page heading, section heading, paragraph, label, and code. Give each a deliberate size and spacing rule. You do not need to copy every one-off size found on the reference page; that often imports accidental inconsistencies into your own design.

Obtain font files from the creator or an authorized distributor and check the license before reuse. A font being downloadable by a browser is not evidence that you can redistribute it. Keep your inspection notes separate from the files you are licensed to ship.

For a wider visual handoff, combine this worksheet with the color palette extraction guide. The useful deliverable is a set of named text roles and verified styles, not a folder of unexplained font filenames.

title: How to Extract a Website Color Palette That You Can Use
description: Find a website’s colors in Chrome, separate CSS values from screenshot samples, and turn the result into a named palette with contrast checks.
body:
To extract a website color palette, inspect the page’s CSS colors, group them by role, and record the foreground/background pairs used together. Chrome’s CSS Overview panel can help you collect page colors. Use the element inspector to confirm each important value before turning the collection into reusable variables.

A useful palette answers “which color goes where?” A long list of hex codes does not. This workflow produces a small palette for surfaces, text, borders, and actions, plus a record of the combinations that need checking.

Decide whether you need CSS values or sampled pixels

Use CSS inspection when you have access to a live page. Use an eyedropper when you are studying a screenshot, illustration, or visible composite. Keep those results labeled separately. Transparency, shadows, and gradients can make a sampled pixel differ from the underlying color declaration.

For example, white text at partial opacity over a dark panel has both a source color and a rendered appearance. Recording only the sampled gray loses the opacity rule. If the panel later changes, that flattened sample no longer describes the intended treatment.

Collect colors with Chrome CSS Overview

  1. Open the page in the theme and viewport you want to study.
  2. Open Chrome DevTools and its command menu.
  3. Search for Show CSS Overview and open that panel.
  4. Select Capture overview.
  5. Review the colors section, then inspect representative elements for the values you plan to keep.

Chrome’s CSS Overview documentation describes its page-level color and font summaries. Treat the capture as an inventory for that page, not proof that you have found every theme, state, or component on the site.

Capture again after opening a modal or switching a theme if those views matter. Record what changed. A green “success” message and a green brand button may share a value while serving different purposes.

Name colors by their jobs

Start with a small worksheet. The following palette is an original teaching example, not an extracted brand palette:

RoleExample valueWhere to inspect
Canvas#0B100CPage background
Surface#18221BCard or menu background
Text#F4F7F1Paragraph on canvas
Muted text#B7C1B9Secondary label on surface
Action#AEDFBBPrimary button
On action#102016Text inside that button

Do not merge colors solely because their hex values look close. First ask whether they represent the same role. Keep separate semantic names if two roles may need to change independently, even when their current values match.

Check combinations, not individual swatches

A color does not pass contrast on its own. Check the text against the surface it actually sits on. WCAG 2.2’s minimum text contrast criterion generally calls for at least 4.5:1, or 3:1 for large text, with defined exceptions. Read the W3C explanation and large-text definition when applying those thresholds.

Chrome’s Color Picker reference describes its contrast controls. Check which contrast model your tool displays; an APCA result is not a WCAG 2.x ratio. For gradients or photographs, examine the backgrounds behind the text across its occupied area.

Keep a matrix of actual combinations: text on canvas, muted text on surface, button text on action, and focus indicator against adjacent colors. Do not label the whole interface accessible after checking only one button.

Export a small set of CSS variables

Here is a reusable starting point for the example palette. It deliberately uses role names so you can change the visual direction without rewriting every component:

:root {
  --canvas: #0b100c;
  --surface: #18221b;
  --text: #f4f7f1;
  --text-muted: #b7c1b9;
  --action: #aedfbb;
  --on-action: #102016;
}
.card { background: var(--surface); color: var(--text); }
.button { background: var(--action); color: var(--on-action); }

Download the example palette CSS or follow the Tailwind token mapping guide to use named values in utility classes.

Avoid the common extraction mistakes

  • Saving only a screenshot: retain CSS values and their roles when you can inspect them.
  • Flattening transparency: record alpha and the background behind it.
  • Ignoring states: inspect hover, focus, selected, and error states that belong in your design.
  • Collecting photo colors as UI tokens: keep editorial imagery separate from interface colors.
  • Copying without a purpose: choose a palette suited to your content and verify your own combinations.

Pair the palette with a typography audit, then place both in the wider design-system inventory. Your final file should tell a builder how to use each color and which combinations still require review.

title: How to Extract a Design System from an Existing Website
description: Audit colors, typography, spacing, and component states on a live website. Build a useful token inventory while separating observations from assumptions.
body:
To extract a design system from a website, inspect representative pages, record recurring styles, group those observations into named tokens, and verify them across components and states. The result is a reconstructed inventory. A live website alone cannot tell you all of the team’s original design decisions, component APIs, or unpublished guidelines.

Start with one useful deliverable: a token sheet plus a few component specifications. You can expand it once you know which rules repeat. Trying to collect every CSS declaration first usually produces more cleanup than insight.

Choose a representative sample

Select pages that exercise different layouts: a marketing page, an article or documentation page, a form, and a list or dashboard if one exists. Within each, inspect a heading, paragraph, link, button, field, card, and navigation item. Record unavailable components as missing evidence, not as invented styles.

Set a clear scope: the viewport, theme, signed-in state, and date. If you have only a homepage, say so. A homepage can provide a visual direction, but it is a weak basis for claiming a complete product design system.

Build an observation inventory

CategoryRecordCheck again on
ColorsValue, alpha, role, paired backgroundText, buttons, alerts, menus
TypographyRendered family, weight, size, line heightHeadings, body, labels, forms
SpacingGap, padding, margin, container widthCards, sections, compact layouts
ShapeBorder widths, radii, shadowsButtons, cards, dialogs
BehaviorFocus, hover, error, disabled statesKeyboard and pointer interaction

Use the dedicated font identification and color palette extraction guides for those passes. Keeping each pass focused makes it easier to compare the same property across several components.

Separate observations from inferred rules

Imagine observing card padding of 16px, 24px, and 32px. You might propose an 8px spacing step, but those three observations do not prove the entire site follows it. A 20px button inset or a fluid section gap could be equally intentional.

Keep two columns: observed value and proposed token. Add a confidence note based on repeated evidence. This is an editorial working method, not a statistical score. For example:

Observation: 24px gap between cards on the listing page
Proposal: space.section-item = 24px
Evidence: repeated in two desktop lists
Open question: mobile list uses a different gap
Decision: keep responsive values separate for now

This record gives the next person a reason for the choice and a way to challenge it. A token name without evidence can turn a guess into a rule that nobody remembers making.

Turn repeated values into meaningful tokens

Separate raw values from intended roles. A raw color might be green.200; a role might be color.action.background. Components should use roles where the meaning is stable. Avoid a token named after a particular position, such as left-card-green, unless that location is the real design concept.

The Design Tokens Community Group format defines a JSON interchange structure with token types, values, and aliases. It is useful when tools need to exchange tokens; it does not automatically reconstruct component behavior from a rendered page.

For a smaller project, a reviewed CSS variable file may be sufficient. MDN’s custom properties guide explains how values can be referenced and scoped. Choose the export format your project will actually maintain.

Write component specifications alongside the tokens

A button needs more than a background token. Document its label style, horizontal and vertical padding, border, minimum dimensions, focus appearance, disabled treatment, and behavior with a long label. Note which details you observed and which you are choosing for your own implementation.

Use a deliberately small validation set: one button, one form field, one card, and a page header. Rebuild them with your token sheet, then compare at narrow and wide widths. When they diverge, inspect the rule responsible instead of adding unexplained magic numbers.

Our CSS inspection guide covers the difference between a declaration in a stylesheet and the resolved styles you see. That distinction matters when a flexible layout produces a pixel width that should not become a fixed token.

Make the handoff usable

Deliver the source URLs and capture conditions, the named token file, component notes, unresolved questions, and a short list of permitted assets. Keep proprietary logos, font files, and illustrations out of a redistribution bundle unless you have the rights to include them.

For Tailwind projects, continue with mapping the inventory into Tailwind v4. For an AI coding workflow, use the DESIGN.md template to explain the decisions and explicitly instruct your agent to read it. A good handoff preserves uncertainty and rationale as carefully as it preserves hex codes.
